facts.value: Quantum cosmology uses a classical notion of spacetime and conceives the whole world as one big wave function expressing the probability of finding particles in a given location.
Cosmogony is the field that studies the origin or creation of the world.
The dominant theory in scientific cosmogony is the Big Bang theory.
According to the Big Bang theory, both space, time and matter have their origin in one initial singularity occurring about 13.8 billion years ago.
This singularity was followed by an expansion that allowed the universe to sufficiently cool down for the formation of subatomic particles and later atoms.
These initial elements formed giant clouds, which would then coalesce into stars and galaxies.
Non-scientific creation myths are found in many cultures and are often enacted in rituals expressing their symbolic meaning.
They can be categorized concerning their contents. Types often found include creation from nothing, from chaos or from a cosmic egg.
Eschatology refers to the science or doctrine of the last things or of the end of the world.
It is traditionally associated with religion, specifically with the Abrahamic religions.
It may include teachings both of the end of each individual human life and of the end of the world as a whole.
It has been applied to other fields as well, for example, in the form of physical eschatology, which includes scientifically based speculations about the far future of the universe.
According to some models, there will be a Big Crunch in which the whole universe collapses back into a singularity, possibly resulting in a second Big Bang afterward.
Current astronomical evidence seems to suggest that our universe will continue to expand indefinitely.
World politics, also referred to as global politics or international relations, is the discipline of political science studying issues of interest to the world that transcend nations and continents.
It aims to explain complex patterns found in the social world that are often related to the pursuit of power, order and justice, usually in the context of globalization.
It considers other transnational actors, like multinational corporations, terrorist groups, or non-governmental organizations.
Examples include the September 11 attacks, the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and the 2008 financial crisis.
Various theories have been proposed to deal with the complexity involved in formulating explanations in world politics.
These theories are sometimes divided into realism, liberalism and constructivism.
Realists see nation-states as the main actors in world politics and constitute an anarchical international system without any overarching power to control their behavior.
Realists are seen as sovereign agents that act according to their national self-interest, with military force playing an important role in the struggle for power between states.
Liberalists acknowledge the importance of states but also emphasize the role of transnational actors.
Liberalists see humans as perfectible and stress the role of democracy in the emergent order of world politics.
Constructivism ascribes more importance to the agency of individual humans than realism and liberalism, understanding the social world as a construction of the people living in it.
Constructivists believe that the international system is an anarchy of nation-states because of human social construction and may change since it is not prefigured by human nature.
